forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
intro: At a St Petersburg fair, a flute sings above the wheeze of an imaginary accordion; street dancers compete for customers, and a magician brings three puppets to life. Ernest Ansermet conducts the original 1911 score, with its unruly piano at the heart of the orchestra.

sections.label: A · Flute above the fair
sections.mNote: Clarinets and horns rock beneath the flute’s tune

sections.label: B · Organ-grinder and music box
sections.mNote: Street entertainers interrupt the crowd’s dancing

sections.label: A′ · The crowd dances again
sections.mNote: The barker calls and the revellers return

sections.label: C · The magician’s flute
sections.mNote: Low bassoons, celesta and harp prepare the spell

sections.label: D · Three puppets dance
sections.mNote: Piano chords and woodwinds set the Russian Dance going

cues.title: Flute above an accordion
cues.text: A flute throws its tune across rocking clarinets and horns. Their alternating fifths and thirds imitate an accordion. Four solo cellos join the commotion: the fair already has several conversations going at once.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe full score, plate R.M.V. 127, p. 7, opening and rehearsal 1. Gerald Larner identifies the accordion figure in his programme note: https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The organ-grinder’s corner
cues.text: The organ-grinder keeps breaking into the crowd music. His little wind band slows to Meno mosso; flutes turn the handle while the clarinets supply the tune. Beside him, a street dancer beats time on a triangle.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, rehearsals 9–13, especially pp. 21–22; stage directions and tempo changes transcribed in Kirchmeyer’s catalogue. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two dancers compete
cues.text: At the other end of the stage, a second dancer starts her music box. The first answers with her triangle, and both acts continue together. Benois and Stravinsky put a small battle for customers inside the larger fair.
cues.evidence: Original stage directions at rehearsals 15–16, transcribed in Helmut Kirchmeyer’s catalogue, K012, “Summary” and “Structures”. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: The revellers come back
cues.text: The organ-grinder and music box fall silent. The barker resumes his sales pitch, and the dancing crowd returns. Stravinsky keeps cutting between the barker’s hurried announcements and the revellers’ familiar tune.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, rehearsals 17–27: the barker’s Stringendo alternates with Come prima for the returning crowd. Stage directions transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Behind the little curtain
cues.text: Two drummers summon the crowd to the puppet theatre. The music slows to Lento: bassoons mutter, the double basses pluck, and celesta and harp scatter little descending figures. The magician has everyone’s attention.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, rehearsals 28–30, pp. 39–41; the drummers’ stage direction precedes the magician’s entrance. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The magician plays
cues.text: The flute cadenza is the magician’s spell. Its runs climb and curl back, almost alone after the bustle of the fair. Stravinsky writes ad libitum, ma non accelerando: freely, without speeding up.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 41, rehearsal 31: “The Magician Plays the Flute”; cadenza marked ad lib. ma non accel. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy’s letter
cues.text: On 13 April 1912, Debussy writes to Stravinsky about this spell: “a sort of magic in sound, a mysterious transformation of mechanical souls that become human”. He singles out the magician’s music for praise.
cues.evidence: Debussy to Stravinsky, 13 April 1912, quoted in French by IRCAM; our translation of “une sorte de magie sonore, de transformation mystérieuse d’âmes mécaniques qui deviennent humaines”. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: The puppets spring to life
cues.text: Petrushka, the Ballerina and the Moor dance together. The piano hammers out chords with the woodwinds, while the strings pluck beneath them. Allegro giusto: after the magician’s freely paced flute, every joint seems to snap into time.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 44, rehearsal 33: Russian Dance, Allegro giusto; piano, woodwinds and pizzicato strings. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Diaghilev hears a puppet
cues.text: In 1910 Diaghilev visits Stravinsky in Clarens expecting sketches for The Rite of Spring. Instead, Stravinsky plays him music about a puppet provoking an orchestra with furious piano arpeggios. Diaghilev wants a whole ballet. The piano keeps its starring part.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky’s retrospective account of Diaghilev’s visit and the projected Konzertstück, reproduced by IRCAM. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

transitions.title: The organ-grinder interrupts
transitions.how: The crowd’s rushing strings keep meeting a slower wind tune, marked Meno mosso. When the organ-grinder settles into his act, the strings die away; flutes repeat their little turns above clarinets and bass clarinet. The triangle supplies the dancer’s beat.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, rehearsals 9–13, especially pp. 21–22. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Drums summon the crowd
transitions.how: The theatre’s drummers cut through the crowd music. At Lento, bassoons begin their crooked little phrase above plucked double basses. Celesta, harp and muted strings join them, then the magician’s flute cadenza clears nearly everything else away.

transitions.title: The piano starts the dance
transitions.how: Harp glissandi and a final flourish of flute finish the spell. A pause separates them from Allegro giusto. The Russian Dance begins with piano and woodwind chords over a low C in the plucked basses; the piano’s running left hand keeps the dance moving between the string strokes.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 43–44, end of rehearsal 32 into 33. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 7–62, rehearsals 1–47. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-fair.txt; groups describe the passage rather than every simultaneous note. Both harps share one stage position.

timeline.note: The opening combines flute figures, clarinet and horn patterns, then solo cellos.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 7; initial active audio and rise through 0:35.

timeline.note: The organ-grinder passage uses repeating wind figures; triangle marks the dancer’s pulse.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 21–22; low relative level from 2:05 and repeating attacks through 2:45.

timeline.note: Returning crowd episodes restore wind figures, brass punctuation and string motion.
timeline.evidence: Rehearsals 17–29; relative level rises at 3:20–3:25 and crests at 3:50–4:00.

timeline.note: The magic trick reduces the orchestra to low wind gestures and delicate keyboard, harp and string colours.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 41, rehearsal 30; 5:18 boundary and sharply reduced brightness at 5:20.

timeline.note: The Charlatan’s flute cadenza has no continuing accompaniment in the score.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 41, rehearsal 31; 5:52 boundary followed by quiet, low-brightness windows. Approximate cadenza placement, not a note alignment.

timeline.note: The puppet-revealing passage restores small, changing instrumental combinations after the flute cadenza.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 42–43, rehearsal 32; changes at 6:34 and 6:48. Not all listed groups sound throughout.

timeline.note: The Russian Dance combines piano and wind attacks over articulated strings.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 44, rehearsal 33; rising level and attack density around 7:10–7:20.

fields.note: Conductor and ensemble are printed on the sleeve and labels. No individual pianist, celesta player, harpist or other orchestral soloist is identified by the consulted carrier or reissue credits; those names remain unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The transferred London LP is expressly labelled Original Edition; Decca’s reissue catalogue corroborates Version 1911. The consulted full score represents that orchestration, not the 1947 revision. The exact early printing reproduced by Dover, and any session-specific corrections to players’ parts, remain unidentified.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying 1911 composition and original 1912 score are public domain in the United States; the ordinary EU life-plus-70 composition term has not expired.
fields.note: Stravinsky died in 1971, giving an ordinary EU term through 31 December 2041. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance, and it does not grant rights in modern editions, stage designs or choreography. The viewable score is hosted in the US; recording-term eligibility below does not clear the underlying composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established.
fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: He could make a roomful of dancers lose their footing with one displaced accent, then write a psalm that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
In St Petersburg, opera was the family business. Stravinsky’s father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. Born in 1882 at Oranienbaum, he entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks showed what he could do with an orchestra in a few minutes. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. Then came a whole ballet, The Firebird. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he remembered the rehearsals ending with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
